overview: AntiBlind is a one-line visual cleaner: on every UpdateEvent it checks isPotionActive(Potion.blindness) and, when the flag is set, removes the effect from the local active potion map with removePotionEffect. The strip is purely client-side; the server keeps the blindness effect and its expiry timer, so no packet leaves the client and the module is invisible to traffic analysis. The only wire interaction is receive-side: S1C metadata carries the entity's potion-effect bitmask, and S1D re-applications are stripped again on the next update tick.

sections.p: The module is the Memeware event pattern at its smallest: a single public Consumer<UpdateEvent> field named eventConsumer0. Module.toggle() calls EventAPI.put(this) on enable, which subscribes the instance to the client's PubSub bus, and the bus invokes every Consumer field whose generic type matches the fired event. The consumer tests mc.thePlayer.isPotionActive(Potion.blindness) and calls mc.thePlayer.removePotionEffect(Potion.blindness.id) (id 15) when true. In the fork's EntityLivingBase, removePotionEffect pulls the PotionEffect out of activePotionsMap and calls onFinishedPotionEffect, which sets potionsNeedUpdate and, because worldObj.isRemote is true on the client, skips the attribute-modifier half entirely; the local DataWatcher potion bitmask is recomputed on the next onUpdate. The blindness overlay in EntityRenderer is driven by isPotionActive, so the black screen and fog vanish the same tick.

Nothing is sent. The server-side player still has the effect: health packets, S1D apply, S1E expire and the S1C metadata bitmask all continue as vanilla. Because the removal only edits the client's activePotionsMap, the divergence is confined to the local render state. If the server re-applies blindness (a new S1D or a refresh), the next UpdateEvent strips it again within a tick, so the effect can never render. A server cannot learn that the effect was removed: no client packet reports potion state, and the S1C stream is server-originated.

The strip is keyed on the local map, so it depends on the effect having been applied client-side first: an S1D that arrives while the module is disabled leaves the overlay until re-enable. removePotionEffect returns the removed effect and the null branch is silent, which is harmless here. Because the consumer runs on UpdateEvent only, the module never touches other players, only the local camera state. There are no settings, no modes and no config surface; the module is unconditional behavior for the render category.

files.label: AntiBlind.java
files.explanation: The whole mechanism in 17 lines: the single Consumer<UpdateEvent> field, the isPotionActive gate and the removePotionEffect call that constitute the module's entire behavior. The field is what Module.toggle() subscribes through EventAPI.put, so this file is also the registration contract.

files.label: Module.java (event subscription contract)
files.explanation: The base class shows the wiring that makes the strip run: toggle() calls EventAPI.put(this) and EventAPI.remove(this) to subscribe and unsubscribe the module instance on the PubSub bus, and the bus dispatches the declared Consumer fields per event. It is the contract that turns a plain field into a per-tick handler.

countering.label: PacketSelfMetadataListener (self metadata consumer)
countering.explanation: The only Grim consumer of self-targeted S1C metadata. It unwraps WrapperPlayServerEntityMetadata for the player's own entity id, strips the pose entry on 1.14+ clients and reads the watcher-0 flags byte to track sprinting, gliding and swimming for prediction. It never reads the potion-effect bitmask and it reacts only to server-originated packets, so the module's local removePotionEffect produces no observable input: the S1C stream Grim sees is identical to a vanilla client's. This entry is the honest boundary for the whole module family: the strip is a render-state edit that no metadata consumer can observe.

countering.label: HawkPlayer (metadata event state)
countering.explanation: Hawk's per-player state object is where S1C metadata lands: PacketConverter8 turns PacketPlayOutEntityMetadata into a HawkAsyncPlayerMetadataEvent, PlayerEventListener.sendMetadataEvent fires it, and HawkPlayer stores the watchable objects, notably isConsumingOrPullingBowMetadataIncluded, which reads the use-item watcher flags for movement checks. No Hawk check consumes the potion-effect bitmask, and every flag Hawk tracks is server-written; a client-side removal of blindness changes none of them. The module therefore cannot disturb any Hawk state, which is the honest framing: the check surface around S1C exists, but none of it is reachable from a local-only render edit.

countering.label: DamageIndicator (S1C health rewrite)
countering.explanation: Photon's S1C-touching module rewrites the health metadata entry on outgoing ENTITY_METADATA packets when the spoofHealth toggle is on, using the version's MetadataPositionIndex. It is the closest thing to a metadata-validating check in the corpus, and it still validates nothing about the client: it mutates the server-to-client stream and has no return channel. The blindness strip emits no packet and rewrites nothing, so the module is invisible to it by construction. The entry documents that even the most S1C-active anticheat surface cannot reach a local potion-map edit.

countering.label: ExemptionSettings (Bukkit metadata hook)
countering.explanation: The only NCP file the S1C corpus lists, and it is not a check: it walks Bukkit entity metadata (hasMetadata) to decide exemption tags for other NCP features. NCP has no metadata-validity check at all, so there is no NCP-side surface the strip could trip. This entry is the honest gap for the anticheat's S1C story: the blindness removal is undetectable by design, and NCP's only S1C touch is a Bukkit convenience hook, not a detector.
